definition: Schenck v. United States, 249 U.S. 47 (1919) is a U.S. Supreme Court decision which found the Espionage Act of 1917 constitutional and established the clear and present danger test for First Amendment violations by the Federal government. The Court ruled that freedom of speech and freedom of the press under the First Amendment could be limited only if the words in the circumstances created a clear and present danger that a crime will occur. If the clear present danger test is satisfied, then the First Amendment does not protect the individual from Government action to prevent the danger. Background Following the United States’ entry into World War I, Congress passed the Espionage Act of 1917 which made efforts to “make or convey false reports or false statements with intent to interfere” with the U.S. military efforts illegal. Charles Schenck, the defendant, printed and mailed leaflets to the public of Philadelphia, PA declaring that the draft violated the Thirteenth Amendment. The leaflets also encouraged citizens who were registered for the draft to peacefully disobey draft orders. Schenck was convicted for violating the Espionage Act. He appealed his conviction, arguing that the Act violated the First Amendment’s protection of freedom of speech and freedom of the press. The Supreme Court unanimously upheld Schenck’s conviction. Justice Holmes, writing for the Court, stated that the Act did not violate the First Amendment, reasoning that Schenck’s intent in sending the pamphlets was to encourage individuals to avoid the draft, which interfered with the United States’ war efforts. Holmes explained that while most speech is typically protected by the First Amendment, there are exceptions. For example, shouting “fire” in a crowded theater is not protected speech. Perhaps under calmer circumstances, the Court conceded, the Act would violate the First Amendment. However, the Court placed considerable weight on the circumstances under which speech was restricted—i.e. the United States’ involvement in an international war.
